items.content:
How I Came Back to Double Cross Vodka.

I was at Pernod Ricard launching Absolut Miami at the Fontainebleau.

We spent $50K to deck out the pool, the bars, the whole nine yards.

And this guy is sitting there buying drinks right underneath our nose — at our own party — promoting his brand. Double Cross.

Met him for five minutes. Didn't think much of it.

Six months later, he convinced me to quit my secure job and join his scrappy startup in New York.

After we lost the founder in an accident, I left. Spent years at larger companies. Got bored. Went looking for something to build again.

And through fate and a few connections, the new owners of Double Cross reached out. The brand had been wiped out during COVID — lost distribution, couldn't import, needed a restart.

So we put together a small team, a three-phase plan, and a commitment to do it more disciplined this time.

That's how I ended up back here.

items.content:
Spirits CEOs say it's a storm. Beer CEOs say it's a sea change. One of them is wrong.

Greg Hughes and the spirits consensus — Suntory Global Spirits — are calling this cyclical. Input costs, post-COVID normalization, discretionary spending compression. The playbook is: hold price, manage inventory, wait it out.

Rahul Goyal at Molson Coors Beverage Company is not waiting. His language around this moment is structural — a "defining moment" for the category. Beer has been losing share for two decades. A cyclical framing doesn't fit that math. Opposite end is Michel Doukeris over at Anheuser-Busch, AB InBev

Then there's Heaven Hill Brands. Kate Latts made a point that doesn't fit either camp cleanly: as a family business, they measure in decades, not quarters. It's a different decision framework entirely. And the long view has an advantage when you are not worried about public markets. 

The structural vs. cyclical read has real stakes. If it's cyclical, you cut costs and protect margin until the volume comes back. If it's structural, you reposition now or you don't reposition at all.

My read: spirits is cyclical. Beer is structural. The problem is that spirits and beer are increasingly fighting for the same consumer.

eAuctions are the most misused tool in the sourcing toolkit... Here's what you need to know.

Most teams reach for eAuctions to "squeeze suppliers"...
  
Then wonder why the savings vanish and the relationship sours.

The same failures play out over and over again:

→ Fuzzy specs, so nobody can bid apples-to-apples
→ Launch day arrives... and nobody shows up (or hates you for it)
→ A strategic partner treated like an interchangeable vendor
→ Weeks of work... Trust quietly torched... Swearing off eAuctions forever.

The tool isn't broken. It's pointed at the wrong target.

The real question isn't "can we auction this?"

For beginners, it's "does this category fit an auction, and did we run the RFP first?"

Here's the shift most teams miss:

Yes, you can run an eAuction instead of an RFP...

For truly commoditized spot buys with decent volumes, it's a fast, repeatable play.

(If "one-off widgets", just use a marketplace!)

But if that's the only way you use them, you're capping the value you can pull out.

Or worse, you'll use them in situations where you're hurting things rather than improving them...
  
The bigger, safer unlock on your learning journey: run the RFP first, and let the eAuction replace the best-and-final-offer process that comes after it.
  
That way you keep a backup position, protect the relationship, and true-up bids before anyone races to the bottom.

items.content:
I see the procurement spend funnel a bit differently than others...

Here's how I break down procurement's spend influence:

→ Total Company Spend
This is everything your company spends money on. Salaries, rent, utilities, software, materials - everything.

→ Addressable Spend
All spend where procurement CAN have an influence. Non-addressable = spend where procurement involvement is useless.

→ Spend Under Management
How much of addressable spend is currently formally under procurement's purview (e.g. via your procurement policy's RACI). This varies and depends on your function's maturity, responsibilities and organizational influence.

→ Spend Under Contract/Strategy
Spend that's actively managed from a strategic procurement standpoint. Where competitive negotiation and value creation happens. How much spend are you running through your classic "7-step procurement process"?

→ Fully Governed Spend
Where procurement can link strategy to realized savings through clear purchasing channels (P2P). Very hard to measure without a spend cube and purposeful mapping of your purchasing channels to your spend category (e.g. commodity codes).

You need Procurement, Accounting, Operations and IT fully aligned to get "Fully Governed Spend"

(You also need a good handle on this to make Intake & Orchestration work, by the way...)

Yet, this is where the magic happens.

Key Insights:

→ Addressable comes BEFORE spend under management scope
→ Just because spend is "addressable" doesn't mean you have jurisdiction/influence over it
→ Procurement's job is moving spend down the funnel systematically to generate value
→ Full governance = strategy linked to realized savings in procure-to-pay processes

The biggest gap?

Most procurement teams measure success on "spend under management" but can't prove value creation.

The real question isn't "how much spend touches procurement?"

It's "how much spend can we prove we're optimizing?"

What does your spend funnel look like?

Doesn't matter if it's different...

What matters is that you have clear/coherent definitions...

And aligned stakeholders 😅

items.content:
A 3-way matched purchase beats a Non-PO Invoice every time:

Why?

When you have a matching purchase order, a Goods/Service Receipt and Invoice (3-way match) before payment, you increase:

➝ Fraud prevention
➝ Duplicate payment risks
➝ Visibility and transparency
➝ Accuracy and error reduction
➝ Efficiency in Dispute Resolution
➝ Financial control (approval of spend)
➝ Timely payment (when the invoice matches...)

But bring this up with folks who don't do it today and... Hear them moan...

"That's overkill."

"Our suppliers won't be able to do that."

"We're already approving the invoices so what's the point?"

Why?

Because 3-way match is harder than a Non-PO Invoice process.

It requires you understand your purchasing profile and purchasing channels consequently.

It requires you educate users and suppliers on these processes.

It requires you plan proactively instead or "reacting urgently."

It requires more knowledge and rigor.

These are all cultural issues. 

These are all change issues.

If you're not doing 3-way matching today, should you turn it on for 100% of your invoices tomorrow? 

No.

That will be a disaster...

But you should be developing a long term change plan to trend towards 3-way match for most of your categories.

One logical bite at a time.

With a 3-way match process, you can automate the end-to-end P2P process!

Not so with Non-PO Invoices.

When you get to the other side, you'll wonder how the heck you were operating with 100% non-PO invoices.

(However, there ARE valid Non-PO invoice exceptions)

items.content:
How are you going to successfully deploy AI Agents if you can't define them in one sentence?

Most procurement leaders can't.

They just know AI agents are supposed to fix everything.

Here's the definition we use at Pure Procurement:

An AI agent (big or small) is a trigger-driven business process that navigates ambiguity to produce a defined outcome inside policy guardrails (guides), using connected systems, data and stakeholders (enablers).

Here are the 5 parts:

→ Trigger — what starts it (a request, a document, a scheduled job)
→ Outcome — the defined result it's working toward
→ Guides — the policy layer constraining behavior
→ Enablers — the systems and data it can call on
→ Process — the reasoning path between trigger and outcome (not a fixed flowchart)

Once you have that, ask 3 questions before you deploy:

1️⃣ Is the path to the outcome ambiguous? If every rule is explicit, use traditional automation, not an LLM agent.

2️⃣ Is a "directionally correct" output recoverable? If a wrong output is catastrophic, raise the bar significantly.

3️⃣ Are the guides clearly defined? An agent without guardrails isn't an agent. It's chaos with a chatbot interface.

Can't answer all 3? It's not ready for production.

We go deeper on this framework (and the AI Agent Studio arms race across S2P platforms) in episode 5 of the ProcureTech Unpacked podcast, out today

→ Your existing tech debt isn't a criteria on the chart

→ Your internal champions and political capital aren't a criteria on the chart

→ Your industry isn't a criteria on the chart

→ Your strategy isn't a criteria on the chart

→ Your budget isn't a criteria on the chart

→ Your spend profile isn't a criteria on the chart
  
The "Best" solution in a box does NOT mean it's the right solution for you.
  
Analyst reports are a starting point for market awareness.

(Gartner will actually be the first to tell you that)
  
They are NOT a substitute for a structured internal evaluation:
 
→ Map your objectives and the capabilities you need to get there (not a requirements wish list)
→ Determine your strategy to acquire these capabilities based on market dynamics
→ Weight vendors against YOUR constraints
→ Test drive with YOUR data, YOUR team, YOUR workflows
→ Reference-check with companies YOUR size and complexity
→ Make your own independent decision...
  
There are no shortcuts in life, people.

You're never going to find answers that lead to competitive advantage in a 2x2 box... 😅

(I really wish you could!)
  
Have you ever had a Magic Quadrant used against you in a stakeholder meeting?

What else do you say to put the 2x2 box back into context?

What did I miss from my list below?
